passage:
Class photo day, Sunflower group. Note by Vinita, class teacher.
Saurabh came in quiet this morning because his best friend was absent. When the photographer called, “Big smile!”, Saurabh pulled his lips wide and showed every tooth, but his eyes stayed flat and his hands stayed stiff at his sides. The photographer said, “Happier!” I stepped in and told Saurabh, “That smile is fine. You don't have to feel happy for a photo.” His shoulders dropped a little. After the photo I sat with him and we drew a card for his friend.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh quiet that morning?
qa.a: Because his best friend was absent.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's wide, toothy smile with flat eyes suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely he was still a bit sad and lonely without his friend and was posing the smile because he was asked to. It could also be that he was simply shy of the photographer and camera.

qa.q: What did Vinita do well when the photographer asked for a happier face?
qa.a: She accepted the posed smile and told Saurabh he did not have to feel happy, which took the pressure off, and then she helped with the real feeling by making a card for his friend. 🙂

qa.q: How might the photographer see Saurabh's stiff smile?
qa.a: The photographer may see it as a bad photo that needs fixing, without knowing that Saurabh was missing his friend that day.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a child's toothy, posed smile on cue that does not match a low mood, and an adult accepting it without insisting he feel happy.

passage: The wedding studio in the kasba smelled of flowers and hot lights. Abhinav, five, had been awake since dawn and his new kurta itched. “Smile, beta!” called the photographer. Abhinav bared his teeth in a tight grin and held it so hard his chin shook. Madhav Chacha, standing beside him, bent down. “You can just stand nicely. No need to be happy for the camera.” Abhinav let his mouth relax into a small, tired smile, and the flash went off. Then Chacha found him a chair.

qa.q: What did Madhav Chacha say to Abhinav before the photo?
qa.a: He said Abhinav could just stand nicely and that there was no need to be happy for the camera.

qa.q: What might Abhinav have been feeling while he held the tight grin?
qa.a: He was probably tired and uncomfortable, since he had been up since dawn and his kurta itched, and he was straining to do what the adults asked. He might also have been nervous under the hot lights with strangers watching.

qa.q: How could Madhav Chacha help Abhinav at the next photo?
qa.a: He could let Abhinav rest first and keep saying a relaxed face is enough, so the photo does not become a test of feeling happy.

qa.q: What would change if the photographer kept shouting “Smile!”?
qa.a: Abhinav would likely keep straining his face and get more upset, and the photos would show a forced grin instead of a tired but real boy.

grounding: A preschooler at a family wedding produces a stiff, toothy smile on cue that does not match his tired mood, and an adult lets him drop it.

passage: Jamal scraped his knee at the playground in Accra and cried all the way home. His big brother Kwame cleaned it and put on a plaster. “Let's send Grandma a picture,” Kwame said, holding up the phone. “Smile!” Jamal squeezed his cheeks up and showed his teeth, though his eyes were still wet. Kwame lowered the phone. “You don't have to smile, little man. You can just wave, or show her your plaster.” Jamal thought, then stuck his leg out proudly, and Kwame took that picture instead.

qa.q: What did Jamal show Grandma in the picture Kwame took?
qa.a: He stuck his leg out to show his plaster.

qa.q: What does Jamal's squeezed smile with wet eyes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was still hurt and a little upset but tried to smile because his brother asked. He may also have wanted to please Kwame, who had just looked after him.

qa.q: What small step helped Jamal most?
qa.a: Kwame offered other choices, a wave or showing the plaster, so Jamal could take part without pretending to feel happy.

qa.q: How might Grandma feel seeing the plaster photo rather than a forced smile?
qa.a: She would likely feel close to Jamal and proud of him, seeing a true moment of a brave boy showing off his knee.

grounding: The toothy posed smile after a hurt shows a mismatch with mood, and the older brother accepts it and offers another way to take part.

passage:
Observation note, Anganwadi centre, written by Kashish (worker).
Today Madhuri, five, stood near the new girl at the sand tray and gave two quick eyebrow flashes, then held up a spoon. The new girl did not look up. Madhuri tried again, brows up and down, and then her smile faded and she stepped back. I knelt and said, “Your eyebrows were saying hello. Try saying it too.” Madhuri whispered, “Hello, want to dig?” The new girl nodded, and they filled the pail together for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Madhuri hold up after her eyebrow flashes?
qa.a: She held up a spoon.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri's smile fade after her second try?
qa.a: She probably felt disappointed and a little rejected because her friendly signal got no answer. She may also have felt unsure whether the new girl wanted to play at all.

qa.q: What worked when the eyebrow flash was missed?
qa.a: Kashish named what the eyebrows meant and suggested adding words, and saying “Hello, want to dig?” made the invitation clear.

qa.q: How might the new girl have experienced Madhuri's first attempts?
qa.a: She was busy looking at the sand, so she likely never saw the quick flashes and had no idea she was being invited.

grounding: The note shows a child using a quick eyebrow flash to invite play, the signal being missed, and a spoken greeting making it clear.

passage: The morning bus to the market stopped outside Sunaina's house, and Himani pressed her face to the window. Sunaina was on her doorstep with a skipping rope. Himani lifted both eyebrows high and dropped them, grinning. Sunaina just kept skipping. Himani did it again, bigger, until her forehead ached. Her grandmother laughed. “She can't see little eyebrows from there. Wave and call her name.” Himani stuck her arm out and shouted, “Sunaina! Skip with me later?” Sunaina looked up and waved the rope.

qa.q: What was Sunaina holding on her doorstep?
qa.a: A skipping rope.

qa.q: What might Himani have been feeling when she flashed her eyebrows bigger and bigger?
qa.a: She was probably excited and eager to be noticed, and a bit frustrated that the signal was not working. It is also possible she was just enjoying making funny faces through the window.

qa.q: What could Himani try the next time a friend is far away?
qa.a: She could wave and call the friend's name straight away, as her grandmother suggested, because a quick eyebrow flash is hard to see from a distance.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina not have reacted at first?
qa.a: She was busy skipping and was too far away to notice a small face signal through a bus window.

grounding: A child uses a brief eyebrow flash to greet and invite a game, it is missed, and a wave and spoken invitation work instead.

passage: On the stairs of their building in Osaka, Hana met Kwame from the fourth floor. She lifted her eyebrows quickly and smiled. Kwame flashed his brows right back. Hana's mother, carrying the groceries, said, “Oh, you two said hello with your faces! Can you say it with words too?” Hana giggled. “Hello, Kwame. Want to race to the landing?” “Hello! Yes!” said Kwame. They thumped up the steps, and at the top Hana flashed her eyebrows again, which now clearly meant, “Again?”

qa.q: Where did Hana meet Kwame?
qa.a: On the stairs of their building in Osaka.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when she flashed her eyebrows at Kwame on the stairs?
qa.a: She was likely happy to see him and feeling playful, using the flash as a friendly hello. It could also have been a small surprise at bumping into him.

qa.q: How did Hana's mother help the greeting?
qa.a: She noticed the face hello and asked the children to say it in words too, which turned the signal into a clear invitation to play.

qa.q: How might Kwame understand Hana's last eyebrow flash at the top?
qa.a: After the race, he would likely read it as “Again?” because they now shared the game, so the same small signal carried a clearer meaning.

grounding: Two children exchange a quick eyebrow flash as hello, and adding spoken words makes the invitation to play clear.

passage:
“Amma, are you cross?”
“Hmm?” Nandini didn't look up from the sewing machine. Her eyebrows were pulled tight together.
Vidya put down her crayon. “Sorry I drew on the newspaper.”
Nandini stopped the machine. “Vidya, what? I'm not cross at all.”
“Your eyebrows went like this.” Vidya squeezed her own brows down hard.
Nandini laughed. “Ah! That's my threading face. This needle hole is so tiny, I have to think very hard.”
“So not angry?”
“Not angry. When I look like that, you can just ask me.”

qa.q: What was Nandini working on?
qa.a: The sewing machine; she was trying to thread a tiny needle hole.

qa.q: Why did Vidya say sorry, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She read Nandini's drawn-together eyebrows as anger and felt worried that she was in trouble for drawing on the newspaper. She could also have been feeling guilty about the newspaper already.

qa.q: What small step did Nandini offer for next time?
qa.a: She told Vidya she could just ask when she sees that face, so Vidya can check instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did the moment look to Nandini?
qa.a: To Nandini it was just a hard moment of concentration, so she was surprised that her face had made Vidya think she was angry.

grounding: A preschooler reads lowered, drawn-together brows as anger and apologises, and her mother explains it was concentration.

passage:
Note for Seema's parents, from Anjali, KG class teacher.
During reading corner I was frowning at a long notice from the office. Seema came up, stood very still and said, “Sorry, Ma'am, I will be quiet.” She had not been noisy at all. I realised she had seen my eyebrows pulled together. I told her, “I'm not angry. This is my thinking face, because this letter is long.” She smiled and sat on my lap to look at the letter. You may notice her apologising at home when faces look serious.

qa.q: What was Anjali frowning at?
qa.a: A long notice from the office.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she stood still and said sorry?
qa.a: She was most likely anxious that her teacher was angry with her, even though she had not been noisy. Another reading is that she was just being careful and polite because the room felt serious.

qa.q: What would you advise Seema's parents after this note?
qa.a: When their face looks serious, they could say what it is, such as “I'm thinking” or “I'm cross about the traffic,” so Seema learns which one it is.

qa.q: How does Anjali see Seema's apology?
qa.a: Anjali sees it as a sign that Seema watches faces closely and assumes a frown means anger at her, which is why she explained her thinking face.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a preschooler reading drawn-together eyebrows as anger and apologising, and being told it was concentration.

passage: Payal ran in from the yard with muddy feet and stopped. Ayesha-didi was at the gate, brows drawn tight, staring at the broken fence. Payal went quiet and tucked her feet under her frock. “Sorry for the mud,” she whispered. Ayesha turned. “Mud? No, chhoti. The goat pushed the fence down again and ate half the spinach. That's why I'm cross.” Payal looked at the fence, then at her sister's face. “Not at me?” “Not at you. Come, hold the rope while I tie it.”

qa.q: What had the goat done?
qa.a: It pushed the fence down again and ate half the spinach.

qa.q: Why did Payal tuck her feet under her frock, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She read her sister's drawn-together brows as anger at her and felt scared that the muddy feet had caused it. She may also have felt a little guilty about the mud already.

qa.q: Which choice by Ayesha helped Payal, and why?
qa.a: Ayesha said clearly what she was cross about and that it was not Payal, then gave her a job, so Payal learned whom the frown was about.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when Payal apologised?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a bit sorry that her frown had frightened her little sister over something that had nothing to do with her.

grounding: A preschooler reads drawn-together brows as anger at her and goes quiet, and is told the anger was about something else.

subtype: Eyes shut against a scary scene [Regulating]
passage: The temple fair had a big screen, and the whole village sat on durries to watch the film. Sonali leaned against her cousin Sahil. When the demon with red eyes came roaring out of the smoke, Sonali squeezed her eyes shut and pushed her face into Sahil's arm. Sahil didn't laugh. He held out his hand. “Squeeze if you want. Tell me when to look, I'll tell you when it's gone.” Sonali gripped his fingers. A minute later he whispered, “Gone,” and she peeped out.

qa.q: Where did the village watch the film?
qa.a: At the temple fair, sitting on durries in front of a big screen.

qa.q: What does Sonali squeezing her eyes shut suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was frightened by the roaring demon and was shutting her eyes to handle the fear. She might also have been startled by the sudden noise more than the picture itself.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that helped?
qa.a: He did not laugh, offered his hand to squeeze, and told her when the scary part was over, so she could cope and come back when ready.

qa.q: What would change if Sahil had teased her for closing her eyes?
qa.a: Sonali might feel ashamed and try to keep watching, which could make her more scared, or she might want to leave the fair.

grounding: A child shuts her eyes during a frightening part of a film to control fear, and an older cousin offers a hand.

subtype: Eyes shut against a scary scene [Regulating]
passage: Rain tapped the window of the flat in Lisbon. Paulo and his mother Beatriz were watching a cartoon about three pigs. When the wolf's shadow slid across the door, Paulo pulled a cushion over his eyes and went very still. Beatriz pressed pause. “That part is scary. Do you want a break, or my hand?” From behind the cushion Paulo said, “Hand. And keep the sound quiet.” She turned the volume down and held his hand. When the pigs cheered, the cushion slowly came down.

qa.q: What did Paulo pull over his eyes?
qa.a: A cushion.

qa.q: What might Paulo have been worried about when the wolf's shadow appeared?
qa.a: He was likely scared that something bad would happen to the pigs and chose to hide his eyes to feel safer. It is also possible the loud music bothered him as much as the picture, since he asked for quieter sound.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Beatriz paused and gave Paulo two choices, a break or her hand, so he could control how much of the fear he faced.

qa.q: How might Beatriz see the cushion over Paulo's eyes?
qa.a: She sees it as a sensible way he is managing his fear, not as silliness, which is why she offered comfort instead of telling him to be brave. 🙂

grounding: A child hides his eyes during a frightening part of a film, and his mother offers a hand or a break.

subtype: Eyes shut against a scary scene [Regulating]
passage: On film afternoon at the community centre, the children watched a story about a lost bear. When the storm scene thundered, Deepika clapped her hands over her eyes and peeped through her fingers, then shut them tight. Mahima, the centre helper, crouched beside her. “Storm's loud, isn't it? You can hold my hand here, or sit by the door with me till it's over.” Deepika chose the hand. She kept her eyes shut through the thunder and opened them when the bear found its cave.

qa.q: Which scene made Deepika cover her eyes?
qa.a: The storm scene, when it thundered.

qa.q: What does Deepika's peeping through her fingers suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she felt scared but also curious, wanting to know what happened while keeping the fear small. She may simply have been checking whether the storm had ended.

qa.q: What would you advise a helper to do when a child hides their eyes at a film?
qa.a: Offer a hand or a short break, as Mahima did, and let the child choose, without telling them to look.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima to watch Deepika through the storm scene?
qa.a: Mahima is likely calm and caring, treating Deepika's shut eyes as a healthy way of coping and staying close until the scary part passes.

grounding: A child covers her eyes during a frightening film scene to manage fear, and an adult offers a hand or a break.

passage:
Note by Jahnavi, KG teacher, Tuesday.
Nandini has been trying to wink all week. Today, while the class planned a surprise card for the cook, she turned to her friend and blinked both eyes hard, twice. Her friend asked, “Is something in your eye?” Nandini looked cross and said, “No! It's a wink, it means secret!” Her friend nodded, and they both giggled. I showed Nandini how to hold one eye shut with a finger while practising. For now, the class has agreed that a double blink means secret too.

qa.q: What was the class planning?
qa.a: A surprise card for the cook.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when her friend asked about her eye?
qa.a: She was frustrated and a bit embarrassed that her wink was misread, because she wanted to share the secret. She may also have felt proud of trying, since she explained what it meant.

qa.q: What small step did Jahnavi try to help Nandini?
qa.a: She showed her how to hold one eye shut with a finger while practising, and let the class accept a double blink as a secret sign.

qa.q: How might Nandini's friend have seen the double blink at first?
qa.a: The friend read it as a problem with her eye, not a signal, because they did not yet share the meaning.

grounding: The note shows a preschooler who blinks both eyes while trying to wink about a secret, and a shared meaning being agreed.

passage: At the weekly haat, Anand Nana bought two jalebis and hid one behind his back. He looked at Vandana and closed one eye slowly. Vandana knew that look meant a treat was coming. She tried to wink back and her whole face scrunched, both eyes shut and her nose wrinkled. Nana laughed so much the shopkeeper laughed too. “That's a very big wink,” he said, and handed her the hidden jalebi. All the way home, Vandana kept practising on the rickshaw, one hand over one eye.

qa.q: What did Anand Nana hide behind his back?
qa.a: A jalebi.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when Nana winked at her?
qa.a: She was likely excited and delighted, because she knew his wink meant a treat was coming. She may also have felt a little shy when the shopkeeper laughed at her big wink.

qa.q: How could Nana help Vandana keep enjoying the wink game?
qa.a: He could keep laughing with her, not at her, and practise the wink together so it stays their shared joke.

qa.q: Why might the shopkeeper see the wink differently from Vandana?
qa.a: The shopkeeper did not share their jalebi game, so he only saw a funny scrunched face, while Vandana knew it meant a treat.

grounding: A preschooler tries to return her grandfather's wink but scrunches both eyes, and the wink works through their shared joke.

passage: Kaito was hiding behind the park slide in Sapporo when Siddiq ran past, counting. Siddiq spotted him, stopped, and winked, then kept running as if he hadn't seen. Kaito grinned. He tried to wink back but blinked both eyes, twice. Later, Siddiq asked, “Why did you blink at me?” “It was a wink! It meant thank you for not telling.” Siddiq laughed. “Mine meant I won't tell.” They decided a thumbs up would be their secret sign, since Kaito's winks still came out as blinks.

qa.q: What did Kaito and Siddiq choose as their secret sign?
qa.a: A thumbs up.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when Siddiq winked and kept running?
qa.a: He felt pleased and relieved that Siddiq was keeping his hiding place secret. He might also have felt a little unsure whether the wink meant Siddiq would come back to catch him.

qa.q: What went well when the wink was misread?
qa.a: The boys talked about what each signal meant and agreed on a thumbs up, which fixed the mix-up without anyone feeling silly.

qa.q: How did Siddiq see Kaito's double blink?
qa.a: He did not understand it, so he asked why Kaito blinked, showing the wink only worked once they both knew its meaning.

grounding: A preschooler finds winking hard and blinks both eyes, while a friend's wink carries a playful secret they both understand.

passage: Nkechi knocked the paint pot over at the childminder's house in Leeds, and green ran across the table. “Nkechi!” Chen said sharply. “Look at me when I'm talking.” Nkechi's chin dropped. She stared at her shoes, her fingers twisting her sleeve, and her eyes filled up. Chen took a breath and crouched down. In a softer voice she said, “It's okay. Paint spills. Let's get a cloth together.” Nkechi still didn't look up, but she nodded and took the cloth Chen held out.

qa.q: What colour paint spilled across the table?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: Why might Nkechi have kept looking down even after Chen softened?
qa.a: She was likely still ashamed about the spill and a bit afraid of being told off again, so looking away felt safer. She could also have been trying not to cry.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Asking her to look up while speaking sharply added pressure; crouching down, using a soft voice and inviting her to clean up together helped her settle.

qa.q: What is it like for Chen when Nkechi's eyes fill up?
qa.a: Chen probably realises her sharp tone was too much for a small child and feels a pull to calm things down, which is why she crouches and softens.

grounding: A preschooler looks down when told off, showing shame or fear, and the adult drops the demand for eye contact and speaks calmly.

passage: In the corridor of the preschool in Aizawl, Lalremsiami pushed a boy to get to the front of the line. Minakshi, her teacher, took her aside to the bench. Lalremsiami hung her head and stared at the floor tiles. Minakshi did not ask her to look up. She sat beside her and spoke quietly. “Pushing can hurt. Next time you can say, ‘Please let me in.’ Can you try that?” After a pause, Lalremsiami nodded at the tiles, then peeked up for a moment.

qa.q: Where did Minakshi take Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Aside to the bench in the corridor.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami have been feeling as she stared at the floor tiles?
qa.a: She was most likely ashamed about pushing and a little afraid of getting into more trouble. Looking down may also have been her way of keeping calm while being corrected.

qa.q: What small step did Minakshi give Lalremsiami for next time?
qa.a: She gave her words to use instead of pushing: “Please let me in.”

qa.q: How might the boy who was pushed see the situation?
qa.a: He was likely hurt or upset at being pushed, and seeing the teacher step in could help him feel that the line is fair and safe.

grounding: A preschooler looks down while being corrected, and the teacher uses a calm tone without demanding eye contact.

passage: I'm Ganga, Abhinav's didi. Yesterday he knocked Dadi's glass off the table and it smashed. Dadi said loudly, “How many times have I told you!” Abhinav went still, and his eyes went straight to the floor. I don't know if he was scared or sorry or both. Dadi saw his face and her voice changed. She said softly, “Come, stand away from the glass. We'll sweep it together.” He still didn't look at her, but he held the dustpan while she swept.

qa.q: What did Abhinav knock off the table?
qa.a: Dadi's glass.

qa.q: What do Abhinav's eyes going straight to the floor suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he felt ashamed or scared after the glass smashed and Dadi's loud words. Ganga cannot be sure, and he may have been a mix of both.

qa.q: What did Dadi's change of voice do?
qa.a: Speaking softly and inviting him to help sweep kept him safe from the glass and let him make amends without being pushed to look up.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when she saw Abhinav's face?
qa.a: She probably felt a pang of regret at having been loud and wanted him to know she was not rejecting him.

grounding: An older sister observes her little brother look down when scolded, and the grandmother switches to a calm, gentle tone.

passage: In the busy Lajpat market lane, Vasudha stopped holding the bag and stared. A woman in a wheelchair was buying bangles, and Vasudha's eyes followed the wheels as they turned. She kept staring even as her mother, Vandana, walked on. Vandana came back and knelt. “You're curious about the wheelchair, na? It helps her move, like our legs help us.” Vasudha nodded, still looking. “When we stare for a long time, people can feel uncomfortable. Can you smile and say hello instead?” Vasudha smiled at the woman, who waved.

qa.q: What was the woman in the wheelchair buying?
qa.a: Bangles.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha keep staring at the wheels?
qa.a: She was curious and interested in how the wheelchair worked. She may also have felt unsure, because she had not seen one up close before.

qa.q: What did Vandana do instead of scolding?
qa.a: She explained kindly what the wheelchair does, said long staring can make people uncomfortable, and suggested smiling and saying hello instead.

qa.q: How might the woman see a child who stares versus one who smiles?
qa.a: A long stare may make her feel watched or different, while a smile and hello treats her like any other shopper.

grounding: A child stares at an unusual sight from curiosity, and her mother kindly explains that staring can make others uncomfortable.

passage:
“Mashi, look! His face has pictures on it!”
Bidisha glanced at the bus stop. A young man had a tattoo of vines along his jaw. Sachin was staring, mouth open.
“It's called a tattoo, Sachin. Lots of people choose them.”
“Does it hurt? Why is it on his face?”
“Good questions. But he can see you staring, and that might feel strange for him.”
Sachin looked at his feet. “Am I bad?”
“No, sona. You're curious. Let's wonder quietly and ask me at home.”
Sachin nodded and gave the man a small wave.

qa.q: What was on the young man's face?
qa.a: A tattoo of vines along his jaw.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when he asked, “Am I bad?”
qa.a: He likely felt worried and a bit ashamed that staring was wrong. Before that, he was curious and excited about the tattoo.

qa.q: How did Bidisha support Sachin's curiosity?
qa.a: She named the tattoo, praised his questions, and suggested saving them for home instead of shaming him.

qa.q: If you were the young man, what would you want?
qa.a: You would probably want to be treated normally, perhaps with a smile or a wave, rather than a long, open-mouthed stare.

grounding: A child stares at an unfamiliar person from curiosity, and his aunt kindly explains why staring can make others uncomfortable.

passage:
Daycare note, written by Rukmini (childminder).
Today Aarti's grandmother came to pick her up. She has a large burn scar on one cheek. Bhupen stared at her all through shoe time, and even followed her to the gate with his eyes. She noticed and looked away. Later, I sat with Bhupen and told him, “You were wondering about her cheek. It's a scar from an old burn, and it doesn't hurt now. Staring can make people feel sad.” He asked if he could say bye to her tomorrow. I said yes.

qa.q: What did Bhupen follow with his eyes?
qa.a: Aarti's grandmother, all the way to the gate.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been thinking while he stared?
qa.a: He was probably curious and puzzled about the scar, wondering what happened. He may also have felt a little worried about whether it hurt.

qa.q: What would you advise Rukmini to do tomorrow when the grandmother comes?
qa.a: Stay close while Bhupen says bye, so it becomes a friendly moment, and praise him quietly for greeting her kindly.

qa.q: What is it like for the grandmother when a child stares at her cheek?
qa.a: She may feel noticed for her scar rather than as a person, which is why she looked away.

grounding: The note shows a child staring from curiosity and a childminder explaining kindly, without shaming, that staring can make others uncomfortable.

passage: “Bath time, Chinmay,” Ramesh called across the flat. Chinmay stood in the doorway, folded his arms and puffed out his cheeks like a balloon. Ramesh looked closer. Chinmay's eyes were twinkling, and one cheek was already leaking air in a giggle. “Oh no,” said Ramesh, “a grumpy frog in my house.” Chinmay burst out laughing and hopped toward the bathroom. Ramesh smiled. On Monday the same puffed cheeks had come with stamping and tears, and that time he had sat with Chinmay instead.

qa.q: What did Ramesh call Chinmay?
qa.a: A grumpy frog.

qa.q: How can you tell that Chinmay was feeling playful, not cross, this time?
qa.a: His eyes were twinkling and he was starting to giggle, which suggests he was feeling playful. On another day the same face came with stamping and tears, which showed real upset.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Ramesh read the twinkling eyes and played along with the frog joke, which turned bath time into a game instead of a fight. 😊

qa.q: Why might Ramesh react differently on a day like Monday?
qa.a: On Monday the puffed cheeks came with stamping and tears, so he treated it as real upset and sat with Chinmay instead of joking.

grounding: A preschooler puffs his cheeks as comic theatre, and his father reads the playful tone and body before responding.

passage:
“Zubin, dinner!” Vikas called.
Zubin puffed out his cheeks and turned away.
“Is that a funny face or a cross face?” Vikas asked.
“Cross!” Zubin's voice cracked. He kicked the carpet. “Mishti knocked my tower down.”
“Ah. That's a real cross face, then.” Vikas sat on the floor. “The tall one with the flag?”
Zubin nodded, cheeks still puffed, fists tight.
“That's annoying. Shall we build it again after dinner?”
Zubin let out his breath. “Only if Mishti doesn't touch it.”

qa.q: Who knocked Zubin's tower down?
qa.a: Mishti.
